item.title: [37★] NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-50μ50μ50\mus stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
item.author: Adam Siegel
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 37 ★

Authors: Adam Siegel

arXiv ID: 2610.28538 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to [[1400,280,≤28]][[1400,280,≤28]][[1400,280,\leq 28]], and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above 10−310−310^{-3} with sub-50μ50μ50\mus stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of 10−1410−1410^{-14}, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.

Adam Siegel

item.title: [23★] Cooling more while dissipating less: anomalous tradeoffs from thermodynamic geometry
item.author: Andrea Canzio, ..., Matteo Scandi, Paolo Abiuso
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 23 ★

Authors: Andrea Canzio, ..., Matteo Scandi, Paolo Abiuso

arXiv ID: 2610.27948 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We show that, starting from the same state, optimal driving can sometimes reach a colder (or hotter) target in the same amount of time while dissipating less energy, or equivalently dissipate the same amount of energy in a shorter time. We study this counterintuitive phenomenon in the slow-driving regime of an open quantum system, where we name it Near-Equilibrium Anomalous Tradeoff (NEAT). We establish necessary conditions for its occurrence and show its underlying geometric origin. While NEAT is reminiscent of the well-known Mpemba effect, the two phenomena are distinct in general. We demonstrate NEAT in an exactly solvable qutrit model, as well as for d-dimensional birth-death dynamics with independently controlled energy levels. Finally, we show how NEAT can improve the performance of Carnot engines.

Andrea Canzio, ..., Matteo Scandi, Paolo Abiuso

item.title: [23★] Hybrid Lattice Surgery between Smooth Boundaries
item.author: Grace Ding, Yanzhu Chen, Sheng-Jie Huang
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 23 ★

Authors: Grace Ding, Yanzhu Chen, Sheng-Jie Huang

arXiv ID: 2610.27556 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We develop smooth hybrid lattice surgery for group surface codes, enabling joint logical measurements through merge and split operations along smooth boundaries. The code patches may correspond to identical or different finite groups, including non-Abelian groups. Our central result is that smooth merge and split realize a logical KKK-coset measurement, where KKK is the subgroup defining the interface. This generalizes the joint logical parity measurement of ordinary surface codes. Using a tensor-network representation, we derive explicit measurement circuits and develop procedures for correcting nonidentity measurement outcomes. We illustrate the framework through a generalized controlled multiplication gate between group surface codes and protocols for preparing the TTT, CZCZCZ, CCXCCXCCX, and CSCSCS magic states, producing resources encoded in one or more Z2Z2\mathbb{Z}_2 surface code patches. Our results show how smooth hybrid lattice surgery broadens the range of logical operations available for group surface codes.

Grace Ding, Yanzhu Chen, Sheng-Jie Huang

item.title: [22★] Polynomial-Time Classical Simulation of BosonSampling under Any Constant-Fraction Photon Loss
item.author: Byeongseon Go, Hyunseok Jeong
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 22 ★

Authors: Byeongseon Go, Hyunseok Jeong

arXiv ID: 2610.27065 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Understanding how photon loss changes the classical complexity of BosonSampling is central to assessing the robustness of near-term photonic quantum advantage. In this work, we present a polynomial-time classical simulation algorithm for lossy BosonSampling that applies whenever a constant fraction of the input photons survives. We consider the standard fixed-loss model, where NNN input photons propagate through an MMM-mode interferometer and exactly N−nN−nN-n photons are lost uniformly at random, leaving nnn surviving photons at the output. For any constant surviving fraction n/N∈(0,1)n/N∈(0,1)n/N\in(0,1), the algorithm samples from a distribution within total variation distance εε\varepsilon of the fixed-loss BosonSampling distribution with probability at least 1−δ1−δ1-\delta over Haar-random interferometers, in time poly(M,N,ε−1,δ−1)poly(M,N,ε−1,δ−1)\operatorname{poly}(M,N,\varepsilon^{-1},\delta^{-1}). We further extend the fixed-loss analysis to the uniform-transmission-loss model and obtain analogous polynomial-time simulability for any fixed transmission rate η∈(0,1)η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). These results substantially extend the known provably simulable regime of n=O(√εN)n=O(εN−−−√)n=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon N}) surviving photons or η=O(√ε/N)η=O(ε/N−−−−√)\eta=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon/N}) transmission rate, and demonstrate that even the experimentally relevant linear-survival regime can admit efficient classical simulation under the conditions considered here.

Byeongseon Go, Hyunseok Jeong

item.title: [15★] Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
item.author: Paolo Facchi, ..., Saverio Pascazio, Antonello Scardicchio
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 15 ★

Authors: Paolo Facchi, ..., Saverio Pascazio, Antonello Scardicchio

arXiv ID: 2610.27872 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the 2k2k2k-th moment of N×NN×NN\times N matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for k>2k>2k>2, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first 1/N1/N1/N correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the 1/N1/N1/N term. At k=2k=2k=2 the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.

Paolo Facchi, ..., Saverio Pascazio, Antonello Scardicchio

item.title: [14★] Sparse block encoding with low subnormalisation for quantum linear solvers on unstructured meshes
item.author: Leigh Lapworth, Jarrett Smalley, Christoph Sünderhauf
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 14 ★

Authors: Leigh Lapworth, Jarrett Smalley, Christoph Sünderhauf

arXiv ID: 2610.27915 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Unstructured meshes are widely used in modelling and simulation in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) due to their geometric flexibility. However, they require an efficient block encoding circuit describing the system. Here, we present a new block encoding methodology for unstructured mesh solvers based on decomposing the system matrix into a sum of 1-sparse matrices. This block encoding is engineered to reduce subnormalisation even in the absence of structure by hiding the contribution of large matrix elements behind others. We investigate three methods of 1-sparse decomposition. Our circuit constructions can optionally take advantage of limited matrix bandwidth and repeated values. For example we consider digitisation (reduced precision), where the number of multiplexed rotation gates is equal to the number of non-unique matrix entries. We evaluate our methodologies using 2D and 3D CFD matrices for unstructured aerofoil meshes, structured cavity, and duct meshes, with and without matrix preconditioning. Our results show that we are able to achieve a block encoding with a near constant subnormalisation factor as the number of matrix preconditioning infill levels increases. This significantly reduces the subnormalised condition number and, in one case, reduces the degree of the QSP polynomial approximation to 1/x1/x1/x by 100,000. Reduced precision digitisation is shown to become more effective as the number of preconditioning infill levels is increased and, in one case, reduces the number of multiplexed rotations from 2,785,576 to 546 whilst maintaining an infidelity of 2.6×10−52.6×10−52.6\times10^{-5} relative to the classical solution. The effect of digitisation on QSVT solutions is demonstrated using 2D and 3D unstructured mesh aerofoil cases. Due to its flexibility and automatic applicability, we believe our 1-sparse decomposition block encoding can offer benefits to other quantum applications.

Leigh Lapworth, Jarrett Smalley, Christoph Sünderhauf

item.title: [11★] Quantum algorithm for high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic differential equations based on Carleman linearization
item.author: Koichi Miyamoto
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 11 ★

Authors: Koichi Miyamoto

arXiv ID: 2610.27416 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Addressing nonlinear numerical problems in quantum computing remains challenging, but several approaches, including Carleman linearization (CL), have been proposed to construct quantum algorithms for such problems. In this work, we develop a CL-based method for a high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic differential equation (SDE) dXt=(A(t)Xt+F(t)X⊗st)dt+B(t)dWt\mathrm{d} \mathbf{X}_t = \left(A(t) \mathbf{X}_t + F(t) \mathbf{X}_t^{\otimes s}\right) \mathrm{d} t + B(t) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_t for an RN\mathbb{R}^N-valued random process Xt\mathbf{X}_t, aiming at quantum speed-up with respect to the dimension NN. We introduce auxiliary processes Yjt\mathbf{Y}^j_t that approximate X⊗jt\mathbf{X}_t^{\otimes j}, derive a linearized system of SDEs for them, and obtain the linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing their expectations. We then apply a quantum ODE solver to it and, from the resulting quantum state, extract an estimate for the expectation of a linear function of Xt\mathbf{X}_t by overlap estimation. We show that, provided the nonlinear and noise terms in the SDE are sufficiently small relative to the linear term, the CL error decreases exponentially with the truncation order JJ in CL, and we can estimate the target expectation with a polylog(N){\rm polylog}(N) number of queries to unitaries encoding coefficient matrices AA, FF, and BB. Finally, we also run a numerical demonstration for an SDE related to Langevin dynamics, observing the exponential decay of the CL error as JJ increases.

Koichi Miyamoto

item.title: [9★] Optimal four-copy detection of the three-tangle and its fault-tolerant cost
item.author: Federico Tomás B. Pérez, ..., Philipp Schleich, M. Cerezo
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 9 ★

Authors: Federico Tomás B. Pérez, ..., Philipp Schleich, M. Cerezo

arXiv ID: 2610.27260 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The three-tangle, τ3\tau_3, is a measure of genuine tripartite entanglement that distinguishes GHZ-type from W-type entanglement in pure three-qubit states. Here, we identify the statistically optimal one-sided four-copy detector of the three-tangle and study its implementation cost. The optimal detector has click probability τ23/48\tau_3^2/48, while previous four-copy constructions achieve τ23/256\tau_3^2/256 and therefore require asymptotically 16/316/3 times as many experimental repetitions. Using the representation-theoretic structure of the problem, we construct an ancilla-free implementation of the optimal detector using 15 CNOT gates, together with an 11-CNOT detector with click probability τ23/96\tau_3^2/96. These results reveal a tradeoff between statistical efficiency and implementation cost, since reducing the number of repetitions requires increasingly expensive circuits. We then show that this tradeoff persists once the circuits are encoded. In a fully fault-tolerant setting, the increased click probability comes with a substantial non-Clifford synthesis cost, while an early fault-tolerant implementation based on TT gates and STAR rotations reduces this overhead at the expense of additional encoded resources. We quantify these costs using both the Steane and [[8,3,2]][[8,3,2]] codes, providing explicit resource estimates for implementing the optimal detector across different computational regimes.

Federico Tomás B. Pérez, ..., Philipp Schleich, M. Cerezo

item.title: [7★] Black Holes are about Quantum Information
item.author: Aude Corbeel, Sebastian De Haro
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: Aude Corbeel, Sebastian De Haro

arXiv ID: 2610.28185 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We review and analyse quantum information-theoretic approaches to black hole evaporation that purport to bring us closer to a resolution of the black hole information paradox. Our focus is on the Page-time paradox and on the contribution of the Hayden-Preskill model to understanding information release under the assumption of unitary evaporation. In this model, the black hole is taken to be a finite-dimensional quantum system whose dynamics can be represented by a quantum circuit, and its information-processing and communication abilities are studied. We identify the assumptions underlying this modelling and highlight two key features, fast scrambling dynamics and entanglement as a resource, that underpin the information release in the model. We argue that this reasoning exemplifies a broader change in how information is used in black hole physics, in which quantum information theory now provides a useful operational modelling framework. This application avoids earlier philosophical objections insofar as it is not based on epistemic ignorance and does not regard information as a substance. This line of reasoning has become central to the debate and, as such, warrants greater attention from the philosophy of physics community.

Aude Corbeel, Sebastian De Haro

item.title: [7★] Certified Non-Degenerate Maximum-Likelihood Benchmarking of Quantum LDPC Decoders
item.author: Michele Banfi, ..., Alberto Tarable, Luca Barletta
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 7 ★

Authors: Michele Banfi, ..., Alberto Tarable, Luca Barletta

arXiv ID: 2610.28008 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The measured logical error rate of a quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code depends on the decoding algorithm. We develop a framework that certifies non-degenerate maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding outcomes on individual sampled shots under circuit-level noise, providing a common reference for comparing decoders and codes. Upper and lower bounds on the minimum correction cost in the true and competing logical classes establish success, failure, or an undecided outcome. Branch-and-bound search refines these intervals while retaining valid bounds under resource limits. Counting the outcomes bounds the empirical ML logical error rate, with interval width equal to the undecided fraction. Results for two bivariate bicycle codes show that best-first ordered statistics decoding (BF-OSD) tracks the non-degenerate ML benchmark closely while leaving some ML-correctable shots.

Michele Banfi, ..., Alberto Tarable, Luca Barletta

item.title: [6★] Complete Modified Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for one-dimensional quantum Spin Chain
item.author: Li Gao, Jingyu Guo, Sihao Wang
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 6 ★

Authors: Li Gao, Jingyu Guo, Sihao Wang

arXiv ID: 2610.28600 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We prove a complete modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with a system-size-independent constant for Chen--Kastoryano--Gilyén Gibbs samplers on one-dimensional spin chain at every fixed positive temperature. The result holds for Hamiltonians with bounded finite-range interactions, including noncommuting and spatially nonuniform interactions. It yields trace and diamond mixing times of order O(logN+log(1/ϵ))O(\log N+\log(1/\epsilon)). The proof establishes complete spatial entropy factorization and absorbs quasi-local errors as conditional relative entropy at the original joint state and reference. The static estimate also yields a system-size-independent CMLSI for the single-site Petz heat-bath and regularised heat-bath dynamics.

Li Gao, Jingyu Guo, Sihao Wang

item.title: [4★] Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware
item.author: Zheng Liang Lim, Hoi-Kwong Lo
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Zheng Liang Lim, Hoi-Kwong Lo

arXiv ID: 2610.28204 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME(5,2)(5,2) state, whose every pair of qubits is maximally mixed so that all its information lives in non-local correlations, could in principle serve as a single shared quantum networking resource for teleporting two unknown qubits in parallel (each via its own Bell measurement and Pauli correction). Nonetheless, its hardware implementations remain scarce despite its theoretical importance. Here, we demonstrate parallel teleportation based on a five-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state, AME(5,2)(5,2), on the superconducting processor ibm_pittsburgh. We construct three-qubit Clifford decoders that extract two Bell pairs using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender-receiver assignments. Using parallelization and classical Pauli frame post-processing, we retain reference-receiver entanglement on both channels after three teleportation rounds. With XY4 dynamical decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, the final entanglement fidelities are 0.704±0.0280.704\pm0.028 and 0.680±0.0220.680\pm0.022, where uncertainties are pointwise 99%99\% confidence-interval half-widths over eight trials. Their lower bounds exceed the separability threshold of 1/21/2. The decoder with lower circuit depth generally retains higher mean fidelity, and XY4 generally improves on XX. These results establish a hardware demonstration of two-channel entanglement transmission through repeated AME-assisted teleportation and provide compact decoding circuits for reconfigurable multipartite communication.

Zheng Liang Lim, Hoi-Kwong Lo

item.title: [4★] The Fer expansion of a driven spin under su(2)\mathfrak{su}(2) operations cannot terminate beyond first order
item.author: Lorenzo Bagnasacco, ..., Vittorio Giovannetti, Kazuya Yuasa
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Lorenzo Bagnasacco, ..., Vittorio Giovannetti, Kazuya Yuasa

arXiv ID: 2610.27979 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The Fer expansion writes the propagator of a driven quantum system as an ordered product of exponentials, each generated by the time integral of an effective Hamiltonian that governs the evolution left over by the previous factors. It can be stopped after finitely many factors whenever this leftover evolution is known in closed form, for instance when the effective Hamiltonian commutes with itself at all times, or precesses about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. For su(2)\mathfrak{su}(2), in any representation, from a qubit to a spin of any size, we resum the Fer recursion into a closed map on curves in R3\mathbb{R}^3. We prove that, for a real-analytic drive, in both cases the expansion stops beyond the first factor only trivially, when the first exponential is already exact.

Lorenzo Bagnasacco, ..., Vittorio Giovannetti, Kazuya Yuasa

item.title: [3★] Structured light for addressable two-qubit gates in medium-sized ion crystals: modeling motional and dephasing errors
item.author: Pablo Viñas, ..., Thomas Monz, Alejandro Bermudez
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Pablo Viñas, ..., Thomas Monz, Alejandro Bermudez

arXiv ID: 2610.28217 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Geometric phase gates with addressed laser radiation are widely used in trapped-ion quantum computers to drive high-fidelity entangling gates on an arbitrary qubit pair of a larger ion chain. Such programmable connectivity exploits the collective phonons to mediate the desired interaction, while simultaneously achieving robustness to their thermal fluctuations by a careful calibration of the gate time with respect to the laser and vibrational-mode frequencies. Crosstalk errors can arise when the spectator qubits, which should ideally remain idle during the gate, are partially driven by the laser fields. The minimal crosstalk, which is set by the laser beam size on the spectator ions, can be achieved when the addressing beams propagate perpendicular to the ion chain. However, this results in exciting the radial phonons, and can complicate achieving high-fidelities as the ion chain grows due to the so-called spectral mode crowding. In this work, we present the theoretical description of a scheme recently implemented by Faorlin et al.al.. This scheme overcomes these complications by engineering addressable state-dependent forces along the ion-chain with laser beams that propagate perpendicular to it through the use of structured light gradients. In this way, one can excite the axial phonons and avoid the spectral mode crowding, while simultaneously minimizing the crosstalk. We present a detailed derivation of the entangling gate scheme, together with analytical closed-form expressions for the leading contribution to the gate error caused by thermal motional fluctuations and dephasing noise. Our results confirm that such fluctuations account for up to 93%\% of the error budget under the operating conditions of the gate implemented by Faorlin et al.al.. We identify target parameters to reduce the motional error from the reported 10−310^{-3} to the 10−510^{-5} level.

Pablo Viñas, ..., Thomas Monz, Alejandro Bermudez

item.title: [3★] Dimension-free marginal inequalities for pure three-party states
item.author: Simon Morelli
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Simon Morelli

arXiv ID: 2610.28162 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The quantum marginal problem, concerned with the compatibility of local and global properties of a multipartite quantum system, is arguably one of the fundamental questions in quantum theory. In this article we introduce a novel family of inequalities bounding the allowed local spectra of a pure tripartite state. The number of inequalities in this family grows with the dimension of the system. Most importantly, the inequalities hold for arbitrary dimensions. For equal local dimension at most 4, they generate the complete set of eigenvalue inequalities.

Simon Morelli

item.title: [3★] Measurement incompatibility in Bayesian quantum estimation beyond quadratic loss
item.author: Francesco Albarelli, Stefano Chessa, Jesús Rubio
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Francesco Albarelli, Stefano Chessa, Jesús Rubio

arXiv ID: 2610.28070 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In single-shot Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation, measurement incompatibility can increase the minimum joint quadratic loss by at most a factor of two relative to the bound obtained by optimising each parameter separately. Using the generalised Barnum--Knill inequality, we establish the same bound for a wider class of additive losses generated by positive score functions, showing that this limitation extends beyond the standard quadratic setting. To illustrate this result, we consider a broad family of periodic losses, including the sine loss sometimes employed in interferometry, and derive the corresponding incompatibility bound for Bayesian multiphase estimation with arbitrary prior knowledge. We further extend the framework to unbounded losses, such as absolute losses; this also recovers the case of quadratic losses.

Francesco Albarelli, Stefano Chessa, Jesús Rubio

item.title: [3★] Trapped-ion-based quantum repeater node across a 17 km metropolitan fiber
item.author: K. Fabitha, ..., V. Krutyanskiy, B. P. Lanyon
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: K. Fabitha, ..., V. Krutyanskiy, B. P. Lanyon

arXiv ID: 2610.27854 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Concatenation of quantum repeater nodes has been proposed as a means to distribute entanglement efficiently across future long-distance networks. Here, we demonstrate a trapped-ion repeater node that establishes photonic entanglement over a 17 km fiber traversing a city, moving beyond laboratory-only prototypes. The node comprises two atomic ions coupled to an optical cavity. First, a detailed characterization is performed of the long fiber channel and of ion-photon entanglement distributed across it. Next, a repeater-node protocol is implemented, achieving entanglement between a local photon and a remote photon with a Bell-state fidelity of 81.6+1.9−1.4%81.6^{+1.9}_{-1.4}\%. These results demonstrate that trapped-ion repeater-node technology can operate over existing city-scale fiber infrastructure and represent a step toward distributed quantum repeater networks.

K. Fabitha, ..., V. Krutyanskiy, B. P. Lanyon

item.title: [3★] Allight: A Perfect Photon Collector
item.author: Dan Porat, Ran Finkelstein, Tal Carmon
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Dan Porat, Ran Finkelstein, Tal Carmon

arXiv ID: 2610.27161 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Collecting photons from quantum emitters remains a key limitation in light-matter interaction because conventional lenses collect light only from one direction. Here, we introduce a perfect light collector by inverse-designing a surrounding dielectric structure that encloses the emitter to increase photon-collection efficiency toward unity. Decomposing the device into several refractive interfaces enables emission collection from the full 4π\pi solid angle with adiabatic reshaping into a collimated beam. We experimentally demonstrate, in two dimensions, the ray bending that collimates omnidirectional emission. Our collector transforms current paradigms for highly efficient photon collection from narrowband, cavity-based techniques into experimentally robust, broadband, non-resonant dielectric devices.

Dan Porat, Ran Finkelstein, Tal Carmon

item.title: [2★] Entanglement Distribution in Quantum Switch Networks: Memory Limits and Achievability
item.author: Lei Hu, ..., Sennur Ulukus, Saikat Guha
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Lei Hu, ..., Sennur Ulukus, Saikat Guha

arXiv ID: 2610.28596 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We study the minimum persistent memory required to distribute a graph state through a quantum switch. Specifically, consider a central switch that assists nn remote users in distributing a graph state, using independently generated user-switch Bell pairs. Since Bell-pair generation is probabilistic, different links generally succeed at different times. When a Bell-pair is generated, the qubits may need to be stored in memory while waiting for other links to succeed. Recently, new protocols have been proposed to reduce this storage overhead by processing and releasing some switch qubits before all Bell links are available. However, these protocols do not characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required at each stage. Moreover, the local-cover method in the state-of-the-art Piecemaker protocol is computationally expensive for general target graphs. In this work, we characterize the minimum persistent switch memory required after any subset of users' Bell links are generated and processed. We then develop an online stabilizer-transition protocol that attains this limit, which can be implemented in polynomial time in the number of qubits nn. Remarkably, this optimal protocol can provide substantial memory reductions over existing heuristic approaches. In particular, for the path graph PnP_n over nn users, Piecemaker protocol requires at least ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor qubits of peak persistent memory for \textitevery Bell-links generation order, whereas under the order (1,2,…,n)(1,2,\ldots,n), our protocol requires only one persistent switch qubit. Finally, the same stabilizer-transition framework also provides a direct forward construction for sequential graph-state generation using the minimum number of quantum emitters, equal to the maximum of the height function.

Lei Hu, ..., Sennur Ulukus, Saikat Guha

item.title: [2★] Floquet ground state order
item.author: Suman Mondal, Paul M. Schindler, Marin Bukov
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Suman Mondal, Paul M. Schindler, Marin Bukov

arXiv ID: 2610.28336 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Clean, interacting, periodically driven systems are believed to thermalize to featureless, infinite-temperature states that preclude the formation of stable ordered states. Here, we show stable quantum order, distinct from prethermal order, and its phase transitions in the ground state of the average-energy operator. Decomposing the time evolution into geometric and average-energy dynamics, we apply Geometric Floquet theory to identify the Floquet ground state. We derive a general variational principle to compute the Floquet ground state in large interacting periodically driven systems, and use it to develop a matrix product state algorithm. In driven nonintegrable chains of more than 100 interacting spins, our numerical simulations exhibit a gapped, area-law entangled Floquet ground state in extended parameter regimes; the ground-state manifold can support both dressed equilibrium order (e.g., Floquet antiferromagnets) and inherently nonequilibrium order (e.g., ground-state time crystals). This quantum order is protected by a finite average-energy gap, which closes at phase transition points upon changing model parameters. We decompose Floquet phases of matter into their equilibrium and nonequilibrium elements: whereas the Floquet ground state at any fixed time is a representative of an equilibrium phase of matter, the nonequilibrium content is entirely produced by the drive holonomy and is geometric. Finally, we identify quasilocal counterdiabatic driving as a mechanism for the stability against heating of gapped Floquet ground states in nonintegrable quantum systems, and argue why Floquet ground states evade the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis. Our work enables the study of interacting nonequilibrium matter deep into the many-body regime, and lays the foundations for the engineering of strongly correlated ordered quantum states.

Suman Mondal, Paul M. Schindler, Marin Bukov

item.title: [2★] The next phase of quantum energy science: from mechanisms to applications
item.author: Florian Metzler, ..., Jonah F. Messinger, Nicola Galvanetto
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Florian Metzler, ..., Jonah F. Messinger, Nicola Galvanetto

arXiv ID: 2610.27165 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

A growing research community spanning quantum batteries, molecular and excitonic energy transport, polaritonics, quantum materials and nuclear control has begun to describe its work in terms of quantum energy or quantum energy science. What connects these otherwise disparate efforts is the deliberate use of quantum states, couplings, collective effects and engineered environments to control energetic states and pathways. A key difference from quantum information science is that the complete quantum state does not always need to be preserved; engineered dissipation or dephasing can even improve the desired outcome. We organize this emerging domain through a framework that connects mechanisms, functions, capabilities, and applications. We identify five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, and Transform) and examine the mechanisms that implement them. item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Samuel A. Engel, ..., Kang-Kuen Ni, Norman Y. Yao

arXiv ID: 2610.27053 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The ability to assemble and reconfigure individual atoms is central to performing quantum science using optical tweezer arrays. Here, we demonstrate parallel omnidirectional atom transport and rearrangement using dynamic holograms generated by a single kilohertz-rate spatial light modulator. By carefully characterizing survival and heating, we show that atoms remain confined even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal has settled, enabling significantly faster transport. Combining these techniques, we assemble ytterbium atoms into a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling. In addition, we demonstrate parallel transport between array layers, combining axial and transverse motion to reconfigure atoms in three dimensions. Our approach is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a method for large-scale SLM-based atom assembly as well as programmable three-dimensional control.

Authors: Julian Kusch, Lauriane Chomaz, Wyatt Kirkby

Abstract:

Motivated by a recent experimental work [arXiv:2608.20327][\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20327}{\text{arXiv:}2608.20327}], we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. arXiv ID: 2610.28453 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and circuit QED quantum computers naturally enable coupled qubit-boson simulations. Boson-fermion interactions arise in quantum field theory, where renormalization is required to obtain finite results. We study one of the simplest examples of a coupled fermion-boson system, the static Yukawa model, on the QSCOUT trapped-ion system. We use similarity renormalization to express the same physics in terms of effective particles described by different values of the renormalization parameter ss. This enables us to map data taken in the window of bosonic occupancy that is experimentally accessible to larger occupancies of distinct effective particles. We use this to study strongly coupled, high-occupancy regimes despite limited readout ranges. Using a trapped-ion qubit-boson device on Sandia National Laboratories' QSCOUT platform, we demonstrate the time evolution of the static Yukawa model.

item.title: [1★] Scrambling Separates Superradiance from Quantum Chaos
item.author: Long-Jie Li, ..., Zi-Min Li, Murray T. Batchelor
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Long-Jie Li, ..., Zi-Min Li, Murray T. Batchelor

arXiv ID: 2610.28412 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Early studies on the Dicke model linked superradiance to quantum chaos, whereas later anisotropic Dicke and Rabi studies reached apparently conflicting conclusions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing global chaos from local instability. Along the isotropic Dicke path, a sweep at fixed low excitation energy crosses both the superradiant boundary and a nearby chaotic window, explaining the reported correlation. However, the anisotropic Dicke model can be chaotic in the normal phase and regular in the superradiant phase, making superradiance neither necessary nor sufficient for global chaos. A fidelity out-of-time-order correlator (FOTOC), in contrast, probes the local stability of the stationary point selected by the initial wave packet. The superradiant transition destabilizes the origin, whereas a change in anisotropy can restore its stability and create displaced saddles. Wave packets centered at these saddles exhibit exponential FOTOC growth even on a classically regular Dicke energy shell with Poisson statistics. This local sensitivity also enables quantitative spectroscopy: combined with the topology of stationary points and local density of states relations, FOTOC dynamics reconstructs the absolute amplitudes of spectral singularities in both models without fitting the density of states.

item.title: [1★] Capturing Open Quantum System Dynamics with Compact Dressed Hamiltonians
item.author: Zachary Giles, Dvira Segal
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Zachary Giles, Dvira Segal

arXiv ID: 2610.28358 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We advance the compact dressed Hamiltonian (CDH) framework to simulate the dynamics of open quantum systems strongly coupled to structured bosonic environments. The CDH approach combines reaction-coordinate mapping with a polaron transformation, incorporating strong system-environment hybridization into a dressed representation before truncating the collective bosonic mode. As a result of this truncation, dynamical features are captured with substantially fewer states than in the original representation. The residual environment is treated using a weak-coupling Markovian quantum master equation. We benchmark the method for spin-boson-type models including a single spin, coupled spins, and spin ensembles, considering both resonant and off-resonant regimes and weak to strong system-bath coupling. Comparisons with hierarchical equations of motion and converged reaction-coordinate calculations demonstrate that the CDH representation systematically approaches the reference dynamics with a compact Hilbert space, accurately reproducing oscillation frequencies, relaxation behavior, and long-time populations over a broad parameter regime. The method further captures cooperative phenomena, including bath-mediated interactions, synchronization between spins, and signatures for collective emission. Beyond efficient time propagation, the CDH framework provides direct access to the spectrum and eigenmodes of the Liouvillian. We demonstrate that slow dynamical modes converge rapidly in the CDH representation, enabling identification of relaxation timescales without fitting time-dependent observables. As a whole, the CDH framework provides an efficient and physical description of strongly coupled open quantum-system dynamics.

Zachary Giles, Dvira Segal

Abstract:

We design a hybrid quantum-classical computational workflow, combining density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, to investigate the electronic properties of CaCuO2, a parent structure of high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Our approach uses a quantum algorithm as an impurity solver that is based on variational quantum compressed time evolution to compute the time-dependent Greens function on an IBM Heron quantum device. Utilizing error mitigation techniques and a Lehmann representation fitting procedure, we extract the density of states from the signal in the accessible time regime. Despite the significant challenges rooted in the residual imprecision of currently accessible NISQ devices, we successfully resolve the characteristic features of the spectral function. However, we find that the required numerical accuracy for full DMFT self-consistency exceeds current hardware capabilities, indicating that practical real-material DMFT applications will necessitate post-NISQ hardware developments.

item.title: [1★] Controlled-Z Gates via Floquet Coupling to Two Auxiliary States in Transmon Circuits

Authors: Yutao Chen, ..., Kai Xu, Heng Fan

arXiv ID: 2610.27834 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for quantum information processing. In transmon circuits, higher excited states provide additional pathways for engineering interactions within the computational subspace. Here we demonstrate controlled-Z (CZ) gates that exploit two noncomputational states, \ket02\ket{02} and \ket20\ket{20}, through selective Floquet coupling. The nontrivial parametric modulation can activate both auxiliary transitions from \ket11\ket{11} while suppressing the leading exchange between \ket01\ket{01} and \ket10\ket{10}. Based on this approach, we develop two gate protocols: a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright auxiliary superposition and adiabatic evolution along a zero-energy dark state, both achieving average gate fidelities above 99.99%99.99\% in numerical simulations. Control of the modulation phase further extends the bright-state protocol to conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates. Effective-model simulations show that unconventional control improves tolerance to residual ZZZZ coupling and static qubit-frequency offsets relative to conventional control over the parameter ranges examined. Simulations including neighboring spectator qubits show that the original nonadiabatic bright-state and adiabatic dark-state CZ protocols retain high gate fidelities. This framework offers new routes toward the experimental realization of CZ gates and their geometric implementations.

item.title: [1★] Active isolation of transmon readout with a tunable inductive bridge
item.author: Chunyang Ding, ..., Konrad W. Lehnert, David I. Schuster
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Chunyang Ding, ..., Konrad W. Lehnert, David I. Schuster

arXiv ID: 2610.27137 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Scalable superconducting quantum computation requires fast, high-fidelity readout. Currently, this is assisted through cryogenic amplification of the readout signal. In traditional dispersive readout schemes, the amplifiers that are used to provide high signal-to-noise ratio also generate thermal noise that can decohere the qubits, demanding additional ferrite-based isolators to suppress this noise. Here, we integrate a chip-scale microwave switch, the tunable inductive bridge, into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon. Flux-pulsing the switch, such that it transmits only during the readout, did not make a discernable difference to qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity metrics. By injecting broadband noise that mimics amplifier thermal photons, we show that the switch suppresses the resulting qubit dephasing by more than 3030~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio, establishing it as a potential chip-based integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators.

item.title: [1★] Cavity models of non-Abelian gauge theories
item.author: Lucia Valor, ..., Stefan Filipp, Peter Rabl
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Lucia Valor, ..., Stefan Filipp, Peter Rabl

arXiv ID: 2610.27070 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In quantum optics and related fields, cavity quantum electrodynamics provides a powerful framework for modeling the low-energy properties of bound charges coupled to electromagnetic fields, using a minimal set of atomic levels and isolated photonic modes. Here, we develop a similar framework for non-Abelian gauge theories, focusing on the pure-gauge dynamics of SU(2) fields as the conceptually simplest example. Starting from the corresponding Yang-Mills Lagrangian, we derive an SU(2) cavity Hamiltonian in the Coulomb gauge, represented in terms of only three localized bosonic modes. Unlike its non-interacting electromagnetic counterpart, this model exhibits a nontrivial excitation spectrum featuring bound composite gauge particles ('glueballs') as the lowest-energy configurations. We extend this framework to one-dimensional arrays of coupled SU(2) cavities and discuss the driven excitation of a glueball condensate and the clustering of multi-glueball states as two elementary interaction-induced processes in these models. These examples offer a glimpse into the multitude of novel many-body phenomena that arise within this cavity SU(2) framework and we show how this physics at the interface between particle physics and quantum optics can be experimentally explored using state-of-the-art superconducting quantum circuits.

Lucia Valor, ..., Stefan Filipp, Peter Rabl

item.title: [1★] Nambu-Goldstone Bosons and Quantum Fisher Information
item.author: Eugene Chen, Daniel Green
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Eugene Chen, Daniel Green

arXiv ID: 2610.27054 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The quantum Fisher matrix and geometric tensor are powerful tools for quantifying the nature of quantum systems. Unfortunately, the formalism needed to compute these quantities is opaque and has limited the development of physical intuition for their behavior, even in the ground state. For quantum systems with continuous symmetries, we know the ground state can be understood in a model-independent and intuitive way from the correlation functions of conserved currents and charges. In this paper, we demonstrate an equivalence between the quantum Fisher matrix associated with the ground states of systems with continuous symmetries and the Nambu-Goldstone. bosons produced by broken generators. We will show that the information metric defined by the Fisher matrix is the same as the Zamolodchikov metric that defines the coset space of the system. Next we show that the Uhlmann curvature associated with multi-parameter estimation is the same as the charge density matrix that defines the difference between type-A and type-B Nambu-Goldstone bosons. We demonstrate these connections in several examples and discuss the generalization to finite temperature.

Eugene Chen, Daniel Green

item.title: [1★] Symmetry and Quantum Interference in the Attosecond Domain
item.author: C. Figueira de Morisson Faria, ..., J. Rivera-Dean, T. Rook
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: C. Figueira de Morisson Faria, ..., J. Rivera-Dean, T. Rook

arXiv ID: 2610.26901 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In this review, we examine the interplay of symmetry and quantum interference in the attosecond domain primarily through one- and two-electron photoelectron momentum distributions. Using our own work, we discuss how tailored laser fields provide control over dynamical symmetries, and how quantum-orbit methods make it possible to connect the resulting momentum-space structures to specific ionisation, propagation, and rescattering pathways. Particular emphasis is placed on ultrafast photoelectron holography and nonsequential double ionisation through recollision excitation with subsequent ionisation, where several distinct forms of quantum interference can be identified and manipulated. We also discuss how target properties, including the binding potential, orbital symmetry and parity, modify this mapping. Finally, we consider emerging opportunities offered by non-classical states of light, for which photon statistics and quantum fluctuations provide additional degrees of freedom for controlling symmetry and strong-field electron dynamics.

item.title: [0★] Cumulative locality governs collective quantum charging
item.author: Sebastián V. Romero, Xi Chen, Yue Ban
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Sebastián V. Romero, Xi Chen, Yue Ban

arXiv ID: 2610.28614 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum batteries can outperform their classical counterparts through collective quantum effects, yet the conditions enabling such advantage remain unclear. Using a generic class of free-fermionic chargers we prove that global operators are insufficient for scalable superextensive charging and that a cumulative hierarchy of many-body operators is required, with the structure of the battery determining the degree of advantage. Not limited to quadratic Hamiltonians, our results establish cumulative locality as a key resource for quantum charging advantage.

Authors: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber

arXiv ID: 2610.28528 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

Authors: Sridevi Kuriyattil, ..., Andrew J. Daley, Pablo M. Poggi

Abstract:

Long-range interactions in many-body quantum systems give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena, from collective dynamics well described by integrable mean-field models with symmetric all-to-all couplings, to fast scrambling of quantum information from disordered long-range interactions. Here, we investigate scenarios in which both regimes emerge within a single deterministic, translation-invariant XY spin model with long-range couplings. We consider a sparse powers-of-two (PWR2) graph, where each spin interacts with a logarithmic number of neighbors, and a power-law-decaying model. By altering the initial state via local perturbations on a completely symmetric state, we show that the dynamics changes from collective to scrambling as witnessed by bipartite and multipartite entanglement measures. We characterize this collective-to-scrambling crossover using Lyapunov exponents in the semiclassical regime, and show that the spectral properties of the coupling graph adjacency matrix provide a very efficient tool to predict the onset of fast scrambling. Our results offer a unified framework for controlling the switch between collective and scrambling dynamics in a setup accessible in experiments with neutral atoms in cavities or in tweezer arrays.

item.author: Long-Jie Li, ..., Zi-Min Li, Murray T. Batchelor
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Long-Jie Li, ..., Zi-Min Li, Murray T. Batchelor

arXiv ID: 2610.28415 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Identifying the quantum signatures of classical chaos remains a central question in quantum physics, and quantum scrambling provides a new perspective on this correspondence. We study two distinct limits of the same model to examine how the correspondence between chaos and scrambling changes across different regimes. The thermodynamic-limit anisotropic Dicke model exhibits a close correspondence between chaos and scrambling, whereas this correspondence breaks down in the large-frequency-ratio limit of the anisotropic Rabi model (ARM). This implies that, in the large-frequency-ratio limit, eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to qualify the ARM as a classically chaotic model. This finding suggests that identifying chaos in quantum systems requires jointly considering the classical degrees of freedom and eigenstate delocalization.

Abstract:

Authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia, ..., Juan Manuel Murillo, Antonio Brogi

arXiv ID: 2610.28342 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

Abstract:

Abstract:

Abstract:

Universal information extracted from entanglement at a critical point is commonly associated with the long-distance properties of the bulk state, while microscopic details of a lattice bipartition are expected to be washed out under coarse graining. Counterintuitively, we show directly that such microscopic information can survive in the statistical ensemble that determines the second Rényi entropy and obviously change the physics there. We interpret this contrast in terms of the Rényi twist defect: the two bipartitions have the same bulk theory but realize different microscopic defect symmetries. Our results demonstrate that lattice information invisible to the bulk continuum theory alone can remain active in the long-distance Rényi ensemble, providing a microscopic explanation for the strong bipartition dependence previously observed in entanglement studies of deconfined criticality.

item.title: [0★] Collision-aware Bayesian mitigation of photon loss in linear optical quantum circuits
item.author: Seungwoo Kim, ..., Hyunho Cha, Jungwoo Lee
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Seungwoo Kim, ..., Hyunho Cha, Jungwoo Lee

arXiv ID: 2610.27529 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Photon loss is the dominant noise source in linear optical quantum circuits. Each lost photon turns an ideal n-photon outcome into a pattern with fewer photons, so the detector counts no longer follow the ideal output distribution, and the lossless events that do follow it become exponentially rare as the photon number grows. Discarding the lossy events (postselection) therefore wastes most of the data at realistic loss rates, and the ideal distribution has to be inferred from the lossy counts themselves. Recycling-based mitigation (Mills & Mezher, Quantum 2026; Quandela's photon_recycling) reweights lossy samples to recover lossless probabilities, but its estimators are biased and restricted to the no-collision sector, where each output mode holds at most one photon. We instead treat the raw counts as Multinomial observations under per-photon binomial loss and infer the ideal output distribution and the loss rate jointly from a Bayesian posterior, which extends naturally to outputs with collisions. On data from the independent Perceval simulator at the scale of prior work (n=4 photons in m=20 and m=10 modes), the posterior has lower KL divergence than both recycling and postselection at every tested loss rate in the no-collision benchmark. In the collision regime it recovers the loss rate and the collision-pattern probabilities, which recycling cannot estimate, and stays below recycling at every loss rate and below postselection except at low loss, where the two are comparable. Its advantage over recycling grows with the sample count, and it supplies credible intervals that the baselines lack.

Abstract:

Quantum and physics-inspired solvers provide specialized sampling interfaces for Ising and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization models, but constrained optimization requires broader coordination and certification. This survey uses classical decomposition to analyze how such solvers can be integrated into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We distinguish formal decomposition, reformulation and reduction, and computational orchestration. For each interface, we ask what the transformation preserves, which assumptions make the outer method converge, and which certificates the implemented inner routine supplies. The central questions are whether that information meets the classical algorithm's requirements and whether hybridization improves solution quality or total cost enough to justify its coordination overhead. Benders decomposition, column generation, graph reduction, and copositive methods illustrate this distinction by separating heuristic proposals from classical certification. We also distinguish component effects within a fixed wrapper, reduction--solver interactions, and comparisons between complete quantum-enabled and classical systems. The analyzed studies provide conditional component benefits and favorable co-design evidence, but do not establish transferable end-to-end superiority over strong classical comparators. The resulting framework identifies opportunities for constraint programming and operations research in structure-preserving design, safeguarded hybrid algorithms, and controlled benchmarking.

Abstract:

We show how adaptive strategies use shots efficiently by concentrating them on assertions with high uncertainty. arXiv ID: 2610.27316 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications rely on elliptic-curve signatures that a quantum adversary breaks and on pseudonym certificates whose anonymity rests on rotation rate, not cryptography. This work presents qDGSP, a post-quantum V2X infrastructure: a hash-based dynamic group signature scheme (DGSP, over SPHINCS+ and WOTS+) distributed between a central controller and roadside verifiers. Group keys derive deterministically from quantum key distribution (QKD) seeds served over the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface, so no group-signature secret crosses the classical channel. qDGSP-EA (Ephemeral Association) binds an ephemeral ML-DSA-65 key to one group signature per 5G cell: messages remain unlinkable across cells, linkable within one. On a testbed with emulated 5G links, median end-to-end latency stayed within the 100ms ETSI budget for every variant. The qDGSP-EA intra-cell DENM matched the NIST ML-DSA-65 baseline on the wire, and under load EA mode raised delivery from roughly 78% to 93%.

item.title: [0★] Counterexamples to the total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture
item.author: Andre Laestadius, Mihály A. Csirik
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Andre Laestadius, Mihály A. Csirik

arXiv ID: 2610.27294 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture asserts that the ground-state particle density and total current determine the scalar potential up to an additive constant and the vector potential up to a gauge transformation. We give three counterexamples for two spinless fermions in the physically relevant setting of three spatial dimensions. In each, a Hamiltonian Hv,AH^{v,\mathbf{A}} has a nondegenerate ground state with identically zero total current but nonzero magnetic field. Complex conjugation then yields a second Hamiltonian Hv,−AH^{v,-\mathbf{A}}, with the same scalar potential and interaction, whose ground state has the same density and the same zero current, while the magnetic field is reversed. The first two examples are noninteracting. One is explicit, with a smooth bounded vector potential and a Gaussian density. The other has smooth bounded scalar and vector potentials in the standard potential spaces. The third example has Coulomb repulsion with unit coupling, an isotropic harmonic scalar potential, and Dirac monopole fields of magnetic charge ±1/2\pm 1/2. The monopole example uses vector potentials defined on separate spatial patches, since these fields are not curls of globally defined smooth vector potentials.

Andre Laestadius, Mihály A. Csirik

item.author: Lawrence M. Qin, ..., Matthew J. Brandsema, Christos Argyropoulos

Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Lawrence M. Qin, ..., Matthew J. Brandsema, Christos Argyropoulos

arXiv ID: 2610.27226 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The ability to efficiently control optical quantum interference by the same device is a challenging task that promises to enable key operations in quantum information processing. Here, we tackle this problem by presenting a composite quantum plasmonic metasurface operating as an ultrathin non-unitary beamsplitter capable of achieving both single photon bosonic bunching and fermionic anti-bunching interference just by varying the incident photons frequency or changing the design dimensions. The presented metasurface combines a plasmonic grating corrugated by periodic nanoslits that can achieve extraordinary optical transmission with additional nanostripes on top forming nanocavities characterized by localized gap plasmon resonances. The photon-photon interactions are analyzed based on calculating the quantum coalescence metric which accurately portrays the obtained bunching or anti-bunching quantum interference. The presented quantum interference operation is applicable to both fundamental non-classical light interactions and in the design of more applied quantum optical logic gates used in quantum computing and communications.

Lawrence M. Qin, ..., Matthew J. Brandsema, Christos Argyropoulos

item.author: Farhad Rasekh, ..., Muralee Murugesu, Daniel Oblak
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Farhad Rasekh, ..., Muralee Murugesu, Daniel Oblak

arXiv ID: 2610.27223 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Rare-earth molecular complexes are attracting increasing interest for quantum information applications because of their structural flexibility and chemical tunability. Here, we compare the cryogenic optical properties of Er3+^{3+}, Tm3+^{3+}, and Eu3+^{3+} complexes in the same ligand environment. Optical spectroscopy shows differing behavior across the three systems: spectral hole burning is observed in the Eu3+^{3+} complex, whereas no measurable hole is detected in the Er3+^{3+} and Tm3+^{3+} complexes. We measure laser-induced local heating and rethermalization in the Er3+^{3+} and Tm3+^{3+} powder-like samples, observing strong local heating and slow thermal relaxation in the cold-plate cryostat. The recovery occurs over several seconds and, for some Er3+^{3+} excitation conditions, extends over tens of seconds. The comparison across the three ions nevertheless suggests that heating alone is unlikely to account for the full contrast. Rather, the different behaviors of Eu3+^{3+}, Tm3+^{3+}, and Er3+^{3+} point to ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence processes associated with their electronic level structure and coupling to the molecular environment. Temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements are further consistent with phonon-mediated broadening through coupling to crystal-field levels.

item.title: [0★] Quantum Fluctuations and Wigner Dynamics of a Carbon Nanotube Oscillator Driven by an Atomic Force Microscope
item.author: Conrad Silio, Cristian Staii
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Conrad Silio, Cristian Staii

arXiv ID: 2610.27167 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Suspended carbon nanotubes provide a useful platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion in regimes where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence can all influence the dynamics. We model the fundamental flexural mode of a carbon nanotube driven by an atomic force microscope as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator subject to a prescribed classical force and coupled linearly to a thermal environment. Starting from the generalized Langevin equation, we formulate the reduced dynamics directly in phase space, where the Wigner function evolves through a Gaussian propagator determined by dissipative linear transport, a deterministic force-induced displacement, and bath-induced fluctuations. For a Drude memory kernel, the retarded response is expressed through the three roots of a characteristic cubic equation. In the classical-noise limit, the three independent entries of the finite-time covariance matrix reduce to explicit finite sums over these response poles, eliminating numerical double-time covariance integration. We extend the construction to the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, obtaining a thermal frequency series representation that retains zero-point and low-temperature fluctuations. For an initial two-packet superposition, we examine interference attenuation and the integrated negative part of the Wigner function, which provides a phase space measure of nonclassicality. These results provide an explicit analytical framework for finite-memory quantum Brownian motion of bound oscillators and a tractable phase space description of driven carbon nanotube dynamics relevant to future quantum state preparation and quantum tomography experiments.

Conrad Silio, Cristian Staii

item.title: [0★] Rényi multi-entropy of graph states and the n−>1n -> 1 limit
item.author: Sriram Akella, Abhijit Gadde
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Sriram Akella, Abhijit Gadde

arXiv ID: 2610.27080 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Rényi multi-entropy extends the Rényi entropy to pure states of more than two parties. It is defined by a replica contraction at integer replica number nn, and the multi-entropy is its n→1n\to1 limit. In holography this limit is conjectured to compute the area of a minimal soap-film web in the bulk. Understanding multi-entropy for general states, however, is harder. Unlike the bipartite case, the replica contraction is not a moment of a density matrix, and the continuation to n=1n=1 has to be found by other means. We study this problem for qubit graph states. We show that at every odd nn the contraction equals 2−k/22^{-k/2}, where kk is a sum of ranks of matrices over a finite field, one row and one column per qubit. We define a class of graphs that we call collision-controlled, for which the rank sum is a polynomial in nn. This class includes graphs without even cycles and all complete bipartite graphs. The natural polynomial n→1n \to 1 continuation is a finite sum over partitions of the parties. While the Rényi multi-entropy is non-increasing under single-qubit Pauli measurements at every odd integer n>1n>1, the continuation to n=1n=1 is not. A ZZ measurement on one qubit of an odd ring with 2r+1≥72r + 1 \geq 7 qubits raises it from (r+1)log2(r+1)\log 2 to (2r−1)log2(2r-1) \log 2. Thus the continuation is not an entanglement monotone.

Sriram Akella, Abhijit Gadde

item.title: [0★] Concurrent Entanglement Purification Scheduling in Dynamic Quantum Networks
item.author: Gongyu Ni, Lester Ho
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Gongyu Ni, Lester Ho

arXiv ID: 2610.26900 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum networks must deliver end-to-end entanglement whose fidelity meets application requirements, which typically requires entanglement purification along multi-hop paths. Existing scheduling approaches either purify at the link level or optimize end-to-end fidelity for a static set of requests, and do not capture concurrent requests competing for network resources over time. This paper studies concurrent entanglement purification scheduling in a time-slotted quantum network with heterogeneous links, in which requests compete for link capacity and quantum memories, and each request may be served by multiple parallel paths for increased reliability. We formulate a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler that maximizes the number of scheduled requests, with max-min path allocation as a fairness criterion, and develop reinforcement learning (RL) schedulers based on DQN, PPO, and SAC, whose rewards balance request success against Bell-pair consumption. Simulations under varying network load, topologies and target fidelity thresholds show that the RL schedulers achieve the highest success rates, improving on MILP by up to 6% and on Progressive Filling and Greedy heuristics by 16.5% and 19.5% respectively, at the cost of higher Bell pair consumption and the deferral of a small fraction of requests. MILP, in contrast, achieves the highest fairness and the lowest Bell pair consumption in most scenarios.

Gongyu Ni, Lester Ho

item.title: [0★] Minimal-length kinematics of coherent light and a proposed two-color vacuum chronoscopy
item.author: Zhi-Wei Wang, Saurya Das, Samuel L. Braunstein
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Zhi-Wei Wang, Saurya Das, Samuel L. Braunstein

arXiv ID: 2610.26892 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The unification of quantum theory and general relativity suggests the existence of a minimal measurable length, leading to a generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) and an energy-dependent vacuum group velocity. Testing these effects with macroscopic objects typically encounters the ``soccer-ball problem,'' where applying Planck-scale deformations to the total momentum predicts observationally ruled-out velocity deviations. We adopt the QFT-natural prescription in which the GUP modifies single-mode commutators, and verify by explicit calculation that the macroscopic group velocity of a multimode coherent pulse reduces to the single-photon GUP velocity evaluated at the central wavelength, multiplied by the classical Gaussian-beam factor, with no dependence on the total pulse energy. The energy--momentum relation E=pcE=pc itself is unmodified; the deformation enters through the velocity--momentum relation and is equivalent to a modified dispersion relation in the wave vector, with a quadratic coefficient that depends on which of the two variables is used. The soccer-ball problem \,---\, which arises only when the GUP is applied to the center-of-mass momentum of a composite system \,---\, is therefore absent for coherent light, and macroscopic petawatt pulses probe the same parameter space as single high-energy photons. Building on this framework, we propose a two-color vacuum chronoscopy experiment using a short-pulse petawatt laser and its high-harmonic generation. By systematically varying the macroscopic beam waist, our setup separates Planck-scale kinematic shifts from classical diffraction delays, establishing a controlled, source-independent terrestrial methodology whose sensitivity we assess against current astrophysical bounds and against the dominant waist-independent systematics that limit it, residual-gas dispersion and the harmonic birth-time offset.

Zhi-Wei Wang, Saurya Das, Samuel L. Braunstein

item.title: [0★] LatticeMind: A Validation-Gated Agentic Framework for Density Functional Theory Workflows
item.author: Nathaniel M. Vegh, ..., Shuaishuai Yuan, Hong Guo
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Nathaniel M. Vegh, ..., Shuaishuai Yuan, Hong Guo

arXiv ID: 2610.26869 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

First-principles calculations are rarely single solver calls: they are multistage workflows in which structures, settings, and saved densities must pass correctly between dependent stages. Language models can write a valid single input, but reliability collapses once stages are chained: a dropped dependency, wrong file handoff, or hallucinated keyword can invalidate results even when the solver runs, and such errors surface only after costly execution. We introduce LatticeMind, a validation-gated agentic framework that converts natural-language requests into executable, checkable density functional theory (DFT) projects. A workflow contract specifies required stages, files, and dependencies; deterministic validators inspect the project before any solver launch; failed checks trigger bounded repair; and reports remain traceable to project files. On a 44-case RESCU benchmark spanning total-energy, density-of-states, band-structure, magnetic, phonon workflows, three non-flagship LLM backends reproduced every reference value; 119 of 132 runs passed on the first validated plan and the rest after one repair cycle. Ablations identify the workflow contract and pre-execution validation as the principal reliability mechanisms; a conventional trial-and-repair baseline reaches 71% at twice the token cost per success. The same architecture reproduces every reference value on a 19-case VASP benchmark, demonstrating transfer across solvers. Beyond these task families, LatticeMind generated and validated the 23 inputs of a multistage study of Rh-induced electronic responses at a Rh6_6/Inx_xGa1−x_{1-x}N photocatalyst interface. These results establish workflow contracts, deterministic validation, bounded repair, and traceable records as a practical foundation for reliable AI-assisted scientific computing, where preventable errors are caught before execution and the solver is never the first validator.

Nathaniel M. Vegh, ..., Shuaishuai Yuan, Hong Guo
